title: THE WOMAN JERICHO CALLED A PROSTITUTE—BUT GOD WROTE HER INTO THE FAMILY LINE OF JESUS
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JERICHO CALLED A PROSTITUTE—BUT GOD WROTE HER INTO THE FAMILY LINE OF JESUS

Rahab lived behind a wall marked for destruction, carrying a name stained by her past. Then faith entered her house—and centuries later, when Matthew opened the story of Jesus Christ, her name was still there.
Imagine hearing that your city is going to die.
The walls that made everyone feel untouchable would fall. The streets you knew would become ruins. The world you had built your survival around was already under judgment.
A woman Scripture does not sanitize.
Joshua 2:1 identifies her with the Hebrew expression אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ’ishah zonah: a woman who was a prostitute.

Some have tried through the centuries to soften Rahab's occupation into something more respectable, such as an innkeeper. But the biblical witness does not need that rescue. The New Testament remembers her with equally unmistakable Greek: Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē, “Rahab the prostitute.”
And remarkably, God was not embarrassed to preserve that description while simultaneously preserving something greater:
The scandal is not that the Bible tells us what Rahab had been.
The scandal is what grace did with her afterward.
Maybe that is why her story can feel uncomfortable.
Because most of us know what it is like to have some word we fear could summarize us.
The thing nobody at church knows.
The thing your family still remembers.
The thing you wish you could remove from your history.
Rahab's story begins with a label too.
But it does not end there.
Two Israelite spies entered Jericho and came to Rahab's house. The king discovered that spies were in the city and demanded that she surrender them.
Suddenly this woman stood at the dividing line between the kingdom she had always known and the God she had only heard about.
And something extraordinary came out of her mouth.
Rahab told the spies that she knew the LORD had given Israel the land. She spoke about the Red Sea. She knew what God had done to Israel's enemies. Jericho had heard the reports.
יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma‘al ve‘al-ha’aretz mittachat.

“The LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
—Joshua 2:11, KJV
A Canaanite prostitute living in a condemned pagan city had come to believe that Israel's God was not merely another tribal deity.
Rahab had heard enough about the LORD to realize that the gods surrounding her were not gods at all.
This is where her story becomes painfully personal.
Rahab had not seen the Red Sea divide.
She had not walked through the wilderness with Israel.
She heard what God had done.
And what she heard produced a decision.
The New Testament later interprets that moment for us: “By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.” —Hebrews 11:31, KJV.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
And biblical faith is not merely agreeing that God exists.

James deliberately points to Rahab when teaching that genuine faith produces action. He says she received the messengers and sent them out another way. James is not teaching that sinners purchase salvation by accumulating good deeds. He is showing that living faith does not remain a lifeless claim. Rahab's actions revealed the reality of the allegiance she professed.
That distinction matters because Christianity is not salvation through moral self-repair.
Clean yourself enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you.

The Gospel is that sinners who cannot rescue themselves are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ. Salvation is by grace through faith, not our works; yet the faith that receives grace begins producing a changed life.
But she could entrust tomorrow to the true God.
The spies promised that when judgment came, Rahab was to gather her family inside her house and tie a scarlet cord in the window.
A red cord hanging against Jericho's wall.
Inside that house were people waiting for mercy while an entire city remained under judgment.

The text does not explicitly call the scarlet cord a symbol of Christ's blood, so we should be careful not to claim something Scripture itself does not directly state. Yet Christians cannot read Rahab's rescue without recognizing the greater biblical reality toward which all salvation ultimately leads: sinners escape final judgment only through God's saving mercy, fulfilled supremely in Jesus Christ.
Rahab's past did not save her.
Her ethnicity did not save her.
Jericho's walls certainly could not save her.
Her hope rested in the promise attached to the refuge God had provided.
And walls that generations probably assumed could never fall...
Think about Rahab in that moment.
The city that had defined her was disappearing.
Yet Joshua 6 records an astonishing exception.
Her brothers and those belonging to her household were brought out.
Joshua 6:25 says that Rahab and her family were spared and that she came to live among Israel.
She went from a condemned city...
into the covenant community of Israel.
to the woman living among God's people.
But God still was not finished writing.
And before Matthew tells us about Bethlehem...
before the Sermon on the Mount...
Because there, in Matthew 1:5, is the name Jericho could never have predicted:
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab...”
Rahab became the mother of Boaz.
And Matthew's genealogy eventually arrives at Jesus Christ.
The prostitute of Jericho appears in the Messiah's family line.
The woman whose city was scheduled for destruction became an ancestor in the line through which the promised Messiah came.
God did not merely pull Rahab from the rubble.
He gave her a future she could never have manufactured.
She entered the genealogy Matthew records on the opening page of the New Testament.
And Hebrews later placed her among examples of faith. James used her as an example of faith demonstrated through action.
Grace gave her story another ending.
That does not mean sin is insignificant.
Grace is breathtaking precisely because sin is deadly.
Jesus did not come to convince us that rebellion against God does not matter. He came because it matters so profoundly that reconciliation required something we could never provide for ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bore sin.
The sinless Son of God died for sinners.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not “pretend your past never happened.”
Bring the part of your testimony you desperately wish belonged to somebody else.
You do not need to make sin beautiful.
You need a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners.
Rahab's story does not teach that everybody automatically receives a happy earthly ending.
Your past does not possess greater authority than God's grace.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years assuming, “God could forgive someone like me, but He could never really use someone like me.”
Perhaps people still remember who you were.
They may even be correct about what you did.
Grace does not require us to rewrite history dishonestly.
David really did commit terrible sin.
The Gospel does not require fake biographies.
Repentance does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings people out of darkness.
That is why your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Still turns testimonies once whispered in shame into evidence that His mercy is stronger than our ruin.
Maybe your Jericho is collapsing right now.
Something you trusted is falling apart.
The carefully constructed version of yourself everyone else believed.
And perhaps beneath all the fear is a realization you have avoided for years:
Do not cling to the wall when God is offering mercy.
And when judgment reached Jericho, she discovered that trusting the true God had changed the trajectory of her life.
If you have never surrendered to Jesus Christ, this is bigger than an inspirational story about overcoming your past.
Confess your sin. Turn from it. Place your trust in Jesus Christ—His death for sinners, His resurrection, His lordship, His mercy.
You do not earn the cross.
You run to the One who died upon it.
And if you already belong to Jesus but shame keeps dragging you back into rooms God has called you out of, remember Rahab.
But to remember who gets the final word over a surrendered life.
Perhaps that is why somebody else needs this article today.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God—it does not.
But if Christ has given us good news, love should make us want other people to hear it.
Let someone who believes they are too dirty for God discover Rahab. Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly how exhausted they are from hiding.
Somebody may be reading silently who desperately needs evidence that Jesus still changes people.
There will be days when old accusations return.
Days when the enemy points backward.
Days when you need to remember a prostitute from Jericho whose name somehow appears in Matthew 1.
If you want to glorify God through generosity, one meaningful way is to help Gospel-centered truth travel farther.
And there is much more waiting for those serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ.
Someone living inside their own Jericho.
Someone convinced their reputation is permanent.
Someone certain heaven could never want their name.
Someone smiling publicly while privately believing they have gone too far.
Rahab's name did not disappear when Jericho's walls disappeared.
Until one day Matthew dipped his pen, began recording the genealogy of Jesus Christ, and wrote a name that should make every ashamed sinner stop breathing for a second:
The woman from the condemned city.
The woman remembered among the faithful.
The woman whose name appears in the family line Matthew traces to Christ.
So when your past whispers, Look what you were...
look toward Jesus and remember what grace can do.
Jericho remembered what Rahab had been; grace carried her name all the way to Jesus.
